text: Day after day they met in the garden, and their love deepened, yet Beatrice never allowed him to touch her, shrinking away with a sad severity whenever his hand drew near. <break time="0.8s" /> She knew nothing of the world beyond the garden walls, and her innocent questions, simple as a childs, made Giovanni forget for a while the dark rumors surrounding her. <break time="0.8s" /> Then Baglioni visited his room and, as if by chance, told an old tale of an Indian prince who sent Alexander the Great a beautiful woman with a breath richer than a garden of Persian roses. <break time="0.8s" /> She had been nourished on poisons from her birth until her whole nature was so steeped in them that her very embrace meant death, and only a wise physician saw through the gift. <break time="0.8s" /> Sensing the professors meaning, Giovanni angrily defended Beatrice, but Baglioni, noticing a faint, strange perfume in the room, declared that her father had made her poisonous through his science. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he drew out a small silver vial, finely carved, and explained that the liquid it held was an antidote so powerful that it could make even the deadliest poisons harmless. <break time="0.8s" /> Give her this, and she may yet be restored to the limits of ordinary nature, he said, and as he went down the stairs, he chuckled at the thought of thwarting Rappaccini at last. <break time="0.8s" /> Left alone with the vial, Giovanni resolved to make a decisive test, for he could no longer endure the doubt whether Beatrice was a heavenly angel or a monster in disguise.
